headline: A coastal storm brings rain this afternoon into early Monday, now trending lighter (only a couple of tenths of an inch for New York City, up to about an inch on eastern Long Island and southeastern Connecticut), and a bigger, more impactful coastal storm looks likely Wednesday night through Friday, with heavy rain on Thanksgiving, gusts of 35–45 mph and widespread coastal flooding.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: Sunday starts with areas of fog and will be unusually mild, with forecast highs of 61 at Bridgeport and 63 at Islip, close to the records of 64 for the date. Some light rain could arrive early afternoon as low pressure moves up the coast, but it mainly comes late afternoon into the evening, moderate to heavy at times in eastern areas. Rain totals keep trending down: only a couple of tenths of an inch around New York City and points north and west, possibly none in the far western areas, and up to about an inch on the forks of eastern Long Island and in southeastern Connecticut, where the heaviest rain falls this evening and overnight (the only area with a marginal risk of flooding rain). Winds turn east and then northeast at 10–15 mph with coastal gusts of 25–30 mph, plus a very low chance of brief 40–45 mph gusts right along the coast of eastern Long Island and possibly southeastern Connecticut if the storm tracks close enough.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: The storm pulls away quickly to the northeast, with any lingering showers ending by daybreak Monday and winds turning light from the northwest. A large, strong area of high pressure moves over the Northeast Tuesday into Wednesday, and conditions look dry Monday through Wednesday. Wednesday night, east-northeast winds pick up with gusts of 23–35 mph possible, and rain may begin as the next storm approaches from the south.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Computer models continue to agree on a potentially large, impactful coastal storm Wednesday night through Thanksgiving and Friday, likely worse for wind and coastal flooding than Sunday's system because it will be pressing against the strong high pressure moving offshore to the north. Gusts of 35–45 mph are possible sometime Thanksgiving Day or Thanksgiving night, and a period of moderate to heavy rain is likely on Thanksgiving, though the storm's fast movement should limit flooding from rain. The pattern is complex enough that small changes could shift the storm's strength, track and timing a lot, so forecasters are still monitoring it.

coast: With Monday morning's high tide, there is at worst a minimal coastal flood threat for the south shore back bays of Nassau County, where minor flood levels may just be touched at the most vulnerable spots; a statement may eventually be needed, though the storm's farther-east track and quick movement could keep water levels short. Tides run high with Tuesday's full moon, so many locations need less than a foot of extra water to reach minor flooding, and the current forecast supports widespread minor to moderate coastal flooding, perhaps even localized major flooding, with the Wednesday night–Friday storm, along with beach flooding, erosion and overwash. On the water, the Gale Watch was dropped as the storm trends east: a Small Craft Advisory runs from 3 PM Sunday to 6 PM Monday for the near-shore ocean waters and from 6 PM Sunday to 6 AM Monday for Long Island Sound, the bays and New York Harbor, and a Gale Warning covers the outer ocean waters from 6 PM Sunday to 6 AM Monday, with rough ocean seas lingering into Monday night. After a brief lull Tuesday afternoon and night, ocean gusts of 29–35 mph (25–30 knots) return by Wednesday afternoon, reaching gale force Wednesday night and storm force on Thursday, with gales reaching the Sound and bays late Wednesday night into Thursday. Waves could build to at least 12–20 feet on the ocean (occasionally 20–25 feet out east), 7–10 feet on western Block Island Sound east of Orient Point, and 4–6 feet on Long Island Sound and at the entrance to New York Harbor.
watch_for: Thanksgiving coastal storm: widespread minor to moderate coastal flooding, possibly locally major, plus beach erosion and overwash, with gusts of 35–45 mph.
Small changes in the Thanksgiving storm's track, strength and timing could make a big difference.
Possible minor flooding on the south shore back bays of Nassau County with Monday morning's high tide.
confidence: Forecasters are fairly confident today's rain will be light around New York City and heaviest out east as the storm trends eastward, and models agree on a significant Thanksgiving storm, but its exact track, strength and timing remain uncertain because of a complex pattern.
